doc.title: Hal Espinosa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 20, 2024

title: Double scale, principal chairs and studio pressure
summary: Hal explains time and a half for principals, double and triple scale, and the pressure on film dates.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: I was talking to Tom Scott on an interview.
And the subject of double scale and maybe triple scale came up. Was that something that the union had a role in?

Yeah in a contract, especially in orchestras and motion pictures, if you’re playing a principal chair it’s always time and a half. No less than time and a half. The contractor would get double scale. And then anybody that — a composer or a conductor wanted specifically and the guy wouldn’t go for time and a half, they could play them whatever they wanted. A lot of guys were getting double time and triple time because they were worth that kind of money to the conductor. And there’s some musicians in L.A., I don’t know about New York I’m assuming New York’s the same, that they won’t work unless

they get double time and they’re working all the time. It’s their reputation and their ability to do the job the first time around. Because when you’re doing a movie date there’s a hundred people on the stage you know in the stage room, and you’re recording, nobody can really make a mistake. If you do you have to stop and then they have to roll the tape back, you have to roll into the movie screen that you have playing behind you for the conductor to follow. So you know they expect you to sight read fly specks. You can’t miss. So guys when they’re that dependable they want ‘em.
That’s high pressure for sure. And I can just picture the contractor like putting a check by someone who made an error. Take him off the list.
